> **A word of advice**
>
> Think of the SCEM labs like going to the gym: if you pay for gym membership but instead of working out you use a machine to lift the weights for you, you won’t get any results.
>
> Generative AI tools can easily provide answers to most of the questions below. But, before you try that, please notice that answering the specific questions below is not the point of this assignment. Instead, the questions are designed to give you the chance to develop a better understanding of estimation concepts and acquire certain _**statistical thinking**_ skills. These are essential skills for any data scientist to be even able to use Gen AI effectively when trying to solve anything non-trivial.
>
> A very important part of this learning involves not having the answers ready-made for you, but instead taking the time to actually search for the answer, trying something, getting it wrong, and trying again.
>
> So, make the best use of this session. The assignments are not marked, so it is much better to try them yourself even if you get incorrect answers (you’ll be able to correct yourself later when you receive feedback) than to have a perfect solution that's not your own.

## Data wrangling with dplyr

### Exercise 1: 

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
Create a new dataset containing only the variables corresponding to `species`, `sex`, `flipper length` and `body mass`. Attribute this new dataset to a variable called `penguins2`.

:::


```{r ex01}
#' Required variables: penguins2 (data.frame)
#' Required plots: 
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins2 <- penguins %>%
  select(species, sex, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)

penguins2
```

### Exercise 5

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
For each (island, species) pair, calculate the number of observations (use `n()`), the mean body mass, the standard deviation of body mass, and the mean flipper length. Store this summary in variable `penguins4`. Check `?mean` and `?sd` to learn how to ignore missing values when calculating the mean / standard deviation.
:::

```{r ex05}
#' Required variables: penguins4 (data.frame)
#' Required plots: 

penguins4 <- penguins %>%
  group_by(island, species) %>%
  summarise(N = n(),
            mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            std_body_mass_g  = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_flipper_len_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))

penguins4
```

## Bayes' theorem

### Exercise 7

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**a.** Write a small function called `bayes_positive()` that takes the prevalence, sensitivity and specificity as input parameters, and returns the posterior probability. A function skeleton is already available below.
:::

```{r ex07a}
#' Required variables: bayes_positive (function)
#' Required plots: 

bayes_positive <- function(prevalence,
                           sensitivity,
                           specificity){
  
  # Enter the body of the function here and
  # don't forget to return() your result.
  
  
}


bayes_positive <- function(prevalence,
                           sensitivity,
                           specificity){
  
  p_positive <- sensitivity * prevalence + (1 - specificity) * (1 - prevalence)
  
  return(sensitivity * prevalence / p_positive)
}

bayes_positive(prevalence = 0.02, sensitivity = 0.95, specificity = 0.98) 
```

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**b.** How does the posterior probability change if the disease is more common? Change the prevalence to `0.2` (i.e., 10 times larger than in the previous example) and check the posterior probability.
:::

```{r ex07b}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: 

bayes_positive(prevalence = 0.2, sensitivity = 0.95, specificity = 0.98) 
```


:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**c.** Now evaluate the posterior probability for the situations indicated in the assignment specs.
:::

```{r ex07c}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: 

# Input data frame
X <- data.frame(prev = c(.01, .05, .2),
                sens = c(.99, .95, .90),
                spec = c(.99, .98, .95))

# Now enter your solution below

# Using mapply()
X$posterior <- mapply(FUN = bayes_positive, 
                      prevalence = X$prev,
                      sensitivity = X$sens,
                      specificity = X$spec)

X
```

### Exercise 8

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**a.** Use `dplyr` to answer the following questions directly from the simulated data:

1. How many individuals tested positive?
2. How many individuals had the disease?
3. Among those with positive tests, how many actually had the disease?
4. Estimate $P(D\mid +)$ 
:::

```{r ex08a}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: 

# Generate simulated population
prevalence  <- .05
sensitivity <- .98
specificity <- .95

# simulated population
population <- data.frame(person = 1:10000,
                         disease = rbinom(10000,
                                          size = 1,
                                          prob = prevalence)) %>%
  mutate(positive = ifelse(disease == 1,
                           yes = rbinom(n(), 1, sensitivity),
                           no  = rbinom(n(), 1, 1 - specificity)))


# Individuals that tested positive (and negative)
population %>%
  count(positive)

# Individuals that actually had the disease (or didn't)
population %>%
  count(disease)

# Among those with positive tests, how many actually had the disease (or didn't)?
population %>%
  filter(positive == 1) %>%
  count(disease)

# You could also get the full truth vs. test table with:
table(population$disease, population$positive, dnn = c("Truth", "Test"))

# Estimate P(D | +)
population %>%
  filter(positive == 1) %>%      # Extract only those that tested positive 
  count(disease) %>%             # Get counts of true and false positives
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%  # Get proportions
  filter(disease == 1) %>%       # Retain only the proportion of correct positive tests
  pull(prop)
```

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**b.** Now modify the simulation so that the disease prevalence becomes **10%**, the sensitivity becomes **90%** and the specificity becomes **95%**. Repeat the calculations with these new parameters. How do these new results compare with the previous simulation?

:::

```{r ex08b}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: 

# Generate simulated population
prevalence  <- .05
sensitivity <- .99
specificity <- .99

# simulated population
population <- data.frame(person = 1:10000,
                         disease = rbinom(10000,
                                          size = 1,
                                          prob = prevalence)) %>%
  mutate(positive = ifelse(disease == 1,
                           yes = rbinom(n(), 1, sensitivity),
                           no  = rbinom(n(), 1, 1 - specificity)))


# Individuals that tested positive (and negative)
population %>%
  count(positive)

# Individuals that actually had the disease (or didn't)
population %>%
  count(disease)

# Among those with positive tests, how many actually had the disease (or didn't)?
population %>%
  filter(positive == 1) %>%
  count(disease)

# Estimate P(D | +)
population %>%
  filter(positive == 1) %>%      # Extract only those that tested positive 
  count(disease) %>%             # Get counts of true and false positives
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%  # Get proportions
  filter(disease == 1) %>%       # Retain only the proportion of correct positive tests
  pull(prop)


## Notice how the precision of the test, P(D|+), also became much better. 

```

## Point estimation of parameters

### Exercise 9

:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**a.** Estimate and plot the sampling distribution of the means of variable `body_mass_g` with `N=10` and `N = 100`, produce a histogram for each case, and check how the standard error of estimation (i.e., the standard deviation of the estimates) changes with the sample size.

:::

```{r ex09a}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: TRUE

# Generate the clea dataset
penguins_clean <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))

library(purrr)
library(palmerpenguins)
nrep <- 1000

sample_means_10 <- map_dbl(.x = 1:nrep,
                           .f = \(i){
                             penguins_clean %>%
                               slice_sample(n = 10) %>%
                               summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g)) %>%
                               pull(mean)})

sample_means_100 <- map_dbl(.x = 1:nrep,
                            .f = \(i){
                              penguins_clean %>%
                                slice_sample(n = 100) %>%
                                summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g)) %>%
                                pull(mean)})


par(mfrow = c(2, 1)) # <--- this changes the plotting device to allow 2x1 panels

hist(sample_means_10, breaks = 25,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the sample mean, N = 10",
     xlab = "Observed sample mean",
     las = 1, 
     xlim = range(sample_means_10))

hist(sample_means_100, breaks = 25,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the sample mean, N = 100",
     xlab = "Observed sample mean",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(sample_means_10)) # <--- note: using the same x limits as the N=10 case for visual comparison of spread

par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # <--- get the plotting device back to normal
```


:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
**b.** Instead of the mean, now generate histograms with the sampling distribution of the _variance_ and of the 90% quantile (check function `quantile()` for this). Notice how not only the estimate values change (as expected), but the _shape_ of the distribution changes: different statistics may have distinct sampling distributions.

:::

```{r ex09b}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: TRUE

sample_stats_10 <- lapply(1:nrep,
                          \(i){
                            penguins_clean %>%
                              slice_sample(n = 10) %>%
                              summarise(var = var(body_mass_g),
                                        q90 = quantile(body_mass_g, probs = 0.9)) %>%
                              select(var, q90)
                          }) %>%
  bind_rows()

sample_stats_100 <- lapply(1:nrep,
                           \(i){
                             penguins_clean %>%
                               slice_sample(n = 100) %>%
                               summarise(var = var(body_mass_g),
                                         q90 = quantile(body_mass_g, probs = 0.9)) %>%
                               select(var, q90)
                           }) %>%
  bind_rows()


# Plot histograms in a 2x2 grid
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)) 

hist(sample_stats_10$var, breaks = 25,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the sample variance, N = 10",
     xlab = "Observed sample variance",
     las = 1, 
     xlim = c(0, max(sample_stats_10$var)))

hist(sample_stats_10$q90, breaks = 25,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the 90% quantile, N = 10",
     xlab = "Observed 90% quantile",
     las = 1, 
     xlim = c(0, max(sample_stats_10$q90)))

hist(sample_stats_100$var, breaks = 25, 
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the sample variance, N = 100",
     xlab = "Observed sample variance",
     las = 1, 
     xlim = c(0, max(sample_stats_10$var)))

hist(sample_stats_100$q90, breaks = 25,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the 90% quantile, N = 100",
     xlab = "Observed 90% quantile",
     las = 1, 
     xlim = c(0, max(sample_stats_10$q90)))


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


## The Central Limit Theorem

### Exercise 10
:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
Generate and visualise the sampling distribution of the means using `nobs=25`, `nobs=50` and `nobs=500`. 
:::

```{r ex10}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: TRUE

# Simulate the population
mypop <- runif(100000)

# Enter your solution below
nreps <- 1000

means <- data.frame(means25 = map_dbl(1:nreps,
                                      \(i) mean(sample(mypop, size = 25))),
                    means50 = map_dbl(1:nreps,
                                      \(i) mean(sample(mypop, size = 50))),
                    means500 = map_dbl(1:nreps,
                                       \(i) mean(sample(mypop, size = 500))))
par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

hist(means$means25, breaks = 30,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sample means (n = 25)",
     xlab = "Sample mean",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(means$means25))

hist(means$means50, breaks = 30,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sample means (n = 50)",
     xlab = "Sample mean",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(means$means25))

hist(means$means500, breaks = 30,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sample means (n = 500)",
     xlab = "Sample mean",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(means$means25))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Exercise 12
:::{#prompt .message style="color: blue;"}
Visualise both the data distribution and the sampling distribution of the means (use `nobs = 15`) of variable `flipper_length_mm` from the `penguins` dataset. Don't forget to `filter()` to remove missing values (`NA`) before you extract your sample means (check the earlier examples in this lab script).
:::

```{r ex12}
#' Required variables: 
#' Required plots: TRUE

mypeng <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm))

nreps <- 1000
nobs <- 15

means15 = map_dbl(.x = 1:nreps, 
                  .f = \(i) mean(sample(mypeng$flipper_length_mm, size = nobs)))

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
hist(mypeng$flipper_length_mm,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Data distribution",
     xlab = "Flipper length (mm)",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(mypeng$flipper_length_mm))

hist(means15, 
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Sample means (n = 15)",
     xlab = "Sample mean",
     las = 1,
     xlim = range(mypeng$flipper_length_mm))
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
```
